svg.text: Hyperstereoscopy: how two 2.5D fields buy a third dimension
Binocular projection yields four coordinates, of which only three are independent; the remaining degree of freedom encodes depth.
1 · One point in the world, two eyes, two projections
the left eye’s 2D field — the near face of its viewing frustum
the right eye’s 2D field — the same, displaced along x
the ray from the world point P to each eye; where it crosses a field is that eye’s dot
the two eyes; each 2D field is the near face of that eye’s frustum
Read it as: a single point P in the shared 3D space projects onto both fields at once. Specifying both
dots takes four numbers — (xₗ, yₗ) and (xᵣ, yᵣ) — but if the dots really do come from one point, the two y’s are the
same. That redundancy is what lets the two fields be matched up and aligned; and the one degree of freedom
left over — the disparity xₗ − xᵣ — is spent on depth. Distance stops being √(x² + y²) and becomes
√(x² + y² + f(z)), so waves that used to spread as circles now spread as spheres.
